spec.cue: Look where it looks. Its two front eyes are sharp in a narrow strip, and it turns them to scan.

fov.note: the wide side eye's span; the whole animal sees nearly all round

rows: The two large front eyes see fine detail, about as sharp as a bird's, and they see it in a narrow strip. In the picture, the sharp middle is a thin upright band.
A narrow strip and a wide sweep
The front eyes each see only a narrow upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and 21 degrees high. The side eyes see a wide span, and only movement draws their attention.
Jumping spiders have green-sensitive and ultraviolet-sensitive receptors in their front eyes, so the picture uses green and ultraviolet where a person sees blue.
The fovea, the gate on still things, the short memory of the picture, and the colour strength are the app's choices. The records do not give these numbers.

claims.how: The record gives 12.5 cycles per degree for the principal eyes of Portia fimbriata.

The side eye field is given as 130 degrees for Metaphidippus aeneolus, and the whole animal's field is given as 360 degrees for salticids in general, so 130 is a relative figure taken from the side eye alone.
UV-sensitive cells with peaks at 330 to 380 nm are recorded for the family, a wider group than the species.

quotes.quote: The highest value of the spatial resolving power (Nyquist frequency) of the principle eyes of jumping spiders, such as Portia fimbriata Doleschell, 1859, is 12.5 cycles/degree
This eye covers a very wide angle (1300), and second-surface refraction is of relatively much greater importance than in the other eye3
Combined, the four pairs of eyes give the spider a 360° field of view.
UV-sensitive cells in Layer IV having peak sensitivity at 330–380 nm
